title: Impact of Peer Ability on Academic Performance

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-Stage Least Squares (Instrumental Variables).  
Why: Roommate ability (z) is randomly assigned and affects the peer-quality variable (x) but plausibly has no direct effect on the student’s GPA other than through x. This satisfies the conditions for a valid instrument.

Key assumptions  
1. Relevance: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 – roommate ability must predict peer quality.  
2. Exogeneity (exclusion): Cov(z, ε) = 0 – random assignment ensures z is uncorrelated with unobserved determinants of GPA.  
3. Stable unit treatment value and linearity in the first and second stages.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Required packages
libs <- c("readr", "AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(lapply(libs, require, character.only = TRUE))

# 1. Read data
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s81_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Naive OLS for comparison
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
cat("\n--- Naive OLS ---\n")
coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))

# 3. First-stage: x on z
fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
cat("\n--- First Stage ---\n")
fs_test <- coeftest(fs, vcov = vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1"))
print(fs_test)
F_stat <- linearHypothesis(fs, "z = 0", white.adjust = "hc1")$F[2]
cat("First-stage F-statistic on instrument (rule-of-thumb > 10):", round(F_stat, 2), "\n")

# 4. 2SLS / IV
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)

cat("\n--- 2SLS / IV Results ---\n")
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))
print(iv_robust)

# 5. Reduced form (placebo / robustness)
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
cat("\n--- Reduced Form (y on z) ---\n")
coeftest(rf, vcov = vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1"))

# 6. Sensitivity: drop controls
iv_nocontrol <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
cat("\n--- 2SLS without Controls ---\n")
coeftest(iv_nocontrol, vcov = vcovHC(iv_nocontrol, type = "HC1"))
```

The code:
• reads the CSV,  
• shows naïve OLS, first-stage strength, and IV estimates with robust (HC1) standard errors,  
• provides reduced-form evidence, and  
• checks robustness by omitting controls.

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive – being exposed to a higher-ability roommate should raise a student’s GPA.  

Magnitude: Roughly 0.20–0.35 GPA points (≈0.2–0.3 standard deviations) per one-standard-deviation increase in peer ability. Random assignment and prior literature on peer effects suggest a modest but economically meaningful effect.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use assigned roommate ability as an instrument for peer quality.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: A positive causal relationship between peer ability and student GPA is identified.
